items.prompt: Put these in the order the incident response lifecycle actually runs: Eradication, Detection & Analysis, Containment, Preparation.
choices: Preparation, Detection & Analysis, Containment, Eradication
Detection & Analysis, Preparation, Eradication, Containment
Containment, Detection & Analysis, Preparation, Eradication
Eradication, Containment, Detection & Analysis, Preparation
items.explanation: Preparation happens before any incident (runbooks, logging, on-call authority already in place). Once something real is suspected, Detection & Analysis confirms and scopes it, Containment stops it from getting worse, and Eradication removes the actual foothold — not just the symptom that triggered the alert. Skipping ahead, e.g. eradicating before scope is confirmed, is one of the most common ways a response makes things worse.
items.reference:
Preparation→Detection & Analysis→Containment→Eradication→Recovery→Post-Incident

Why: each phase depends on the one before it actually being done, not skipped.

items.prompt: Dana's team wants to skip straight from "we found the compromised account" to rotating every credential in the company, without first confirming what the account actually had access to. What's the risk of skipping the analysis/scoping step this way?
choices: There's no risk — more rotation is always safer
They may rotate the wrong things while missing the actual blast radius, and waste response time and trust on changes that don't address what was really exposed
Credential rotation is impossible without first eradicating
Skipping analysis speeds up containment with no downside
items.explanation: Analysis exists to make containment and eradication targeted instead of a panicked guess. Rotating everything feels thorough but can burn time and goodwill on systems that were never touched, while the actual scope — what this specific account could reach — goes unconfirmed. Scoping should start wide and narrow with evidence, not skip straight to an unfocused response.
items.reference:
Preparation→Detection & Analysis→Containment→Eradication→Recovery→Post-Incident

Why: each phase depends on the one before it actually being done, not skipped.

items.prompt: What does the Post-Incident Activity phase feed back into, and why does that matter?
choices: Nothing — it's the last step, purely a record for legal purposes
Preparation — the blameless review's findings (like a service account's over-broad scope) become the concrete improvements the next incident starts from
It feeds back into Detection & Analysis only, to re-check the same incident
It feeds back into Containment, to decide whether to re-isolate the same system
items.explanation: The lifecycle is a loop, not a line: the point of the post-incident review is that its action items (tightening a scope, adding a missing alert) become part of the Preparation the team has in place for whatever happens next — otherwise the incident is survived but nothing durable is learned from it.
items.reference:
Preparation→Detection & Analysis→Containment→Eradication→Recovery→Post-Incident

Why: each phase depends on the one before it actually being done, not skipped.

items.prompt: Dana's 2:14am fork was: isolate the compromised account now, or watch it a while longer. What does watching longer actually buy, and what does it cost?
choices: It buys nothing and costs nothing — the outcome is the same either way
It can buy a cleaner forensic picture of what the attacker is doing, at the cost of letting confirmed data exfiltration continue during that window
It buys faster eradication and costs extra logging overhead
It buys regulatory compliance and costs nothing
items.explanation: The trade-off is real, not a formality: watching a live, compromised session can capture volatile evidence (memory, exact tooling, full attacker behavior) that vanishes the instant the connection is cut — but every extra minute is also more data the attacker can take, if exfiltration is actively happening.
items.reference:
Kill now

Stops the leak, may lose volatile evidence and tip off the attacker

Watch first

Clean forensic picture, but exfiltration continues meanwhile

Why: you usually cannot fully get both benefits at once.

items.prompt: Why can't a team usually get both a clean forensic picture AND stop the breach immediately?
choices: Because forensic tools are always too slow to run in real time

Because volatile evidence (live memory, an active session's exact behavior) typically only exists while the compromised system keeps running — cutting it off to stop the damage destroys that evidence in the same action
Because legal teams forbid running both at once
Because it's actually always possible to get both, this is a myth
items.explanation: The two goals compete for the same resource: the live, connected state of the compromised system. Preserving it for evidence requires leaving it running and connected; stopping the damage requires cutting that connection. There's no action that does both simultaneously — only a judgment call about which one matters more given what's actually at stake.
items.reference:
Kill now

Stops the leak, may lose volatile evidence and tip off the attacker

Watch first

Clean forensic picture, but exfiltration continues meanwhile

Why: you usually cannot fully get both benefits at once.

items.prompt: Northlake's actual case was a slow, low-volume nightly trickle, already durably logged. Which side of the fork does that push toward, and why?
choices: Toward watching longer, because slow trickles are never urgent
Toward isolating immediately — the logs already captured what mattered, so waiting longer gains little while more data keeps leaving every night
Neither — the decision is unrelated to volume or logging
Toward escalating to law enforcement before making any technical decision
items.explanation: The fork isn't decided by volume alone, but by what's actually gained by waiting. Once request logs already durably captured the attacker's activity, watching longer adds little forensic value while every additional night adds more confirmed data loss — so the case for immediate containment wins.
items.reference:
Kill now

Stops the leak, may lose volatile evidence and tip off the attacker

Watch first

Clean forensic picture, but exfiltration continues meanwhile

Why: you usually cannot fully get both benefits at once.

items.prompt: What does "dwell time" mean in an incident response context?
choices: How long the post-mortem meeting lasts
How long an attacker has active, undetected access before containment
How long it takes to patch the vulnerability that was exploited
How long a customer waits for a support response
items.explanation: Dwell time is specifically the undetected window — from initial compromise to containment. It's the single biggest lever on total damage: Northlake's 11-day dwell time is what let a slow trickle add up to thousands of exposed records, when a 1-day dwell time on the same trickle rate would have meant a small fraction of that.
items.reference:
Northlake: 11 nights undetected → ~3,650 records vs. a 1-night dwell time on the same rate → ~330 records

Why: dwell time directly multiplies total exposure.

items.prompt: Two companies suffer breaches with the exact same exfiltration rate per day. Company A detects and contains in 2 days; Company B takes 20 days. What's the single biggest reason their total exposure differs so much?
choices: The attacker's skill level, which is unrelated to detection speed
Dwell time — the same daily rate compounds very differently over 2 days versus 20 days of undetected access
The size of each company's customer base, unrelated to detection speed
Whichever company has better lawyers
items.explanation: With an identical daily rate, total exposure is a direct function of how long the attacker went undetected — dwell time. Company B's 10x longer dwell time means roughly 10x the exposure at the same rate, independent of anything about the attacker's skill or the companies' size.
items.reference:
Northlake: 11 nights undetected → ~3,650 records vs. a 1-night dwell time on the same rate → ~330 records

Why: dwell time directly multiplies total exposure.

items.prompt: When scoping an incident, should the suspected blast radius start narrow and widen only if evidence demands it, or start wide and narrow as evidence comes in?
choices: Start narrow (assume the smallest plausible impact) and widen only if forced to
Start wide (assume everything the confirmed compromise could plausibly reach) and narrow as evidence actually rules parts of it out
It doesn't matter which direction scoping goes
Blast radius should never change once first estimated
items.explanation: Starting narrow and only widening under pressure means a team is systematically likely to under-scope — missing real exposure until forced to admit it. Starting wide and narrowing with actual evidence is the safer default: it costs some extra caution early, but it doesn't let a team assume away exposure it hasn't actually ruled out.
items.reference:
svc-enrollment-export could read every enrollment table — scope started at "all of it," narrowed to the 11 nights' actual records once logs confirmed the real footprint

Why: under-scoping is the more dangerous failure mode.

items.prompt: svc-enrollment-export had read access to every enrollment table, but logs showed it only actually queried one table's worth of records during the incident. What should the blast-radius scoping conclude?
choices: The blast radius is defined purely by what the account could technically reach — every table it could read must be treated as potentially exposed until evidence rules a given table out
The blast radius is only what was actually queried, full stop, no further checking needed
Blast radius is irrelevant once containment has happened
The blast radius should be assumed to be zero until a regulator says otherwise
items.explanation: Scoping starts from capability (what the account could reach), not just observed behavior, because logs can be incomplete or the attacker may have accessed things through a path that wasn't fully logged. Evidence can narrow the scope down from "everything it could reach" to "what we can confirm it actually touched" — but that narrowing has to be earned by the evidence, not assumed from the start.
items.reference:
svc-enrollment-export could read every enrollment table — scope started at "all of it," narrowed to the 11 nights' actual records once logs confirmed the real footprint

Why: under-scoping is the more dangerous failure mode.

items.prompt: What makes a breach "material" in the sense that matters for disclosure obligations?
choices: Any security event at all, no matter how small, is automatically material
It's significant enough — by scale, sensitivity of the data involved, or a specific regulatory definition — to trigger a legal disclosure obligation
Only breaches that make the news are material
Materiality is decided entirely by the engineering team, not legal
items.explanation: "Material" is a threshold concept, not "any incident happened." A blocked login attempt with no data accessed is a security event but almost never material; ~3,650 exposed enrollment PII records including EU residents clears the bar under GDPR. What counts as material is usually a legal/regulatory determination, informed by the technical scoping, not decided by engineering alone.
items.reference:
Blocked login attempt, no data touched → not material. ~3,650 PII records exposed, EU residents included → material under GDPR

Why: materiality is a threshold, not a binary "something happened."

items.prompt: Who typically makes the final call on whether a given incident is "material" enough to trigger legal disclosure?
choices: The on-call engineer who first detected it
Legal/compliance, informed by the technical scope engineering provides — it's a legal determination built on technical facts, not a purely technical one
Whoever is available first, regardless of role
The affected customers themselves, by request
items.explanation: Engineering's job is to establish the facts (scope, data types, number of records, timeline) as accurately as possible; legal/compliance applies those facts against the relevant regulatory definitions to determine materiality and disclosure obligations. Neither can do the other's job — technical scoping without legal judgment risks over- or under-disclosing, and legal judgment without accurate scoping is guessing.
items.reference:
Blocked login attempt, no data touched → not material. ~3,650 PII records exposed, EU residents included → material under GDPR

Why: materiality is a threshold, not a binary "something happened."

items.prompt: A breach exposes 12 internal test records with no real customer data. Is this automatically material under a GDPR-style framework?
choices: Yes — any unauthorized access is automatically material regardless of what was exposed

Not automatically — materiality generally turns on real personal data and realistic risk to individuals, so synthetic test data with no real customer PII is unlikely to clear that bar, though the team should confirm rather than assume
It's material only if more than 1,000 records are involved, always, in every framework
Materiality never depends on what kind of data was exposed
items.explanation: Materiality frameworks generally key on real personal data and realistic risk to individuals, not just "was anything accessed." Twelve synthetic test records likely don't clear that bar — but the team confirms this rather than assuming it, since "test data" sometimes turns out to contain real information copied in from production by mistake, which is itself worth checking.
items.reference:
Blocked login attempt, no data touched → not material. ~3,650 PII records exposed, EU residents included → material under GDPR

Why: materiality is a threshold, not a binary "something happened."

items.prompt: What's the practical difference between Containment and Eradication in the lifecycle?
choices: They're the same step, just different names for the same action
Containment stops the immediate damage (revoke access, block the source); Eradication removes the attacker's actual foothold so they can't just come back the same way
Eradication always happens before Containment
Containment is a legal step; Eradication is a purely technical one
items.explanation: Containment is the fast, defensive move — cutting off what's actively causing harm right now. Eradication is the more thorough follow-up: making sure whatever let the attacker in (a reused credential, a planted backdoor, an over-broad scope) is actually removed, not just the specific session that got noticed. Doing containment without eradication just delays the same incident from recurring.
items.reference:
Containment: revoke svc-enrollment-export credentials, block source IP. Eradication: rotate every credential the account could read, audit for planted persistence

Why: stopping the symptom isn't the same as removing the cause.

items.prompt: Northlake revoked the compromised account's credentials at 02:41 (containment) but didn't rotate every credential the account could have read until later, during eradication. Why not do both instantly at 02:41?
choices: It was an oversight and should have all happened simultaneously with no reason for the gap
Containment needed to happen fast to stop the immediate leak; full eradication requires knowing the true scope of what the account could reach, which took a bit longer to confirm
Rotating credentials is technically impossible during containment
Legal required a mandatory waiting period between the two steps
items.explanation: Containment prioritizes speed on the one clear, urgent action (cut off the active session). Eradication is deliberately a bit slower because doing it well requires knowing the real scope — rotating credentials for systems that were never actually at risk wastes response capacity, while missing ones that were is dangerous. The sequencing reflects different priorities at each phase, not sloppiness.
items.reference:
Containment: revoke svc-enrollment-export credentials, block source IP. Eradication: rotate every credential the account could read, audit for planted persistence

Why: stopping the symptom isn't the same as removing the cause.

items.prompt: What does the Recovery phase specifically watch for, beyond just "things are back to normal"?
choices: Nothing extra — recovery just means turning services back on
The same access pattern recurring — recovery includes heightened monitoring specifically aimed at catching the attacker trying to come back the same way
Only whether customer complaints have stopped
Whether the on-call rotation schedule needs to change
items.explanation: Recovery isn't just flipping services back on — it deliberately keeps monitoring turned up, watching for the specific pattern that was just fixed (in Northlake's case, a similar overnight export anomaly) in case eradication missed something or the attacker tries a variant of the same approach.
items.reference:
Containment: revoke svc-enrollment-export credentials, block source IP. Eradication: rotate every credential the account could read, audit for planted persistence

Why: stopping the symptom isn't the same as removing the cause.

items.prompt: According to the containment decision tree, when does it make sense to briefly preserve a compromised session instead of isolating immediately?
choices: Never — isolate immediately in every case, with no exceptions
When there's genuinely volatile evidence (like live memory or an active connection) worth capturing AND it has real legal/forensic value AND the exfiltration isn't active/high-volume
Whenever the on-call engineer personally prefers to observe longer
Whenever the attacker's identity is already known
items.explanation: The tree's "preserve" branch is narrow on purpose: it only applies when volatile evidence would genuinely be lost by cutting the connection, that evidence actually has forensic/legal value, and the exfiltration isn't actively high-volume (where every minute of delay costs more than the evidence is worth). Preference alone isn't one of the conditions.
items.reference:
Active, high-volume exfiltration → isolate now. Slow/durable-logged trickle → isolate now. Unclear + genuine volatile-evidence value → brief, time-capped preservation first

Why: preservation is the narrow exception, not the default.

items.prompt: Northlake's runbook caps any evidence-preservation window at 15 minutes rather than leaving it open-ended. Why put an explicit cap on it?
choices: Because forensic tools always finish in exactly 15 minutes
Because an open-ended "just a bit longer" window tends to keep extending under pressure, and a fixed cap forces the decision back to containment instead of indefinitely delaying it
Because regulations legally mandate a 15-minute maximum for every company
The cap has no real purpose, it's arbitrary
items.explanation: Without an explicit cap, "let's watch a little longer to be sure" is exactly the kind of decision that quietly extends under real pressure — each additional minute feels justified in the moment. A fixed cap forces a concrete return to the containment decision rather than letting the preservation window drift indefinitely while data continues to leave.
items.reference:
Active, high-volume exfiltration → isolate now. Slow/durable-logged trickle → isolate now. Unclear + genuine volatile-evidence value → brief, time-capped preservation first

Why: preservation is the narrow exception, not the default.

items.prompt: An incident has slow, already-durably-logged exfiltration — the same profile as Northlake's actual case. What does the decision tree say to do, and why doesn't the "unclear, preserve first" branch apply here?
choices: Preserve first, because any uncertainty at all should trigger the preservation branch

Isolate immediately — the "preserve first" branch only applies when it's genuinely unclear AND volatile evidence would answer that uncertainty; here the logs are already durable, so nothing is unclear that preservation would resolve
Escalate to law enforcement before doing anything else
Wait for legal sign-off before taking any containment action
items.explanation: The "preserve first" branch exists to answer a genuine open question using evidence that would otherwise be lost. When the logs already durably captured what happened — as in Northlake's case — there's no open question preservation would resolve, so the tree routes straight to isolating, since waiting longer only costs more exposure with nothing gained.
items.reference:
Active, high-volume exfiltration → isolate now. Slow/durable-logged trickle → isolate now. Unclear + genuine volatile-evidence value → brief, time-capped preservation first

Why: preservation is the narrow exception, not the default.

items.prompt: Which audience typically gets told first, and why?
choices: Customers, because they have the most at stake
Internal exec/legal, because they're the ones who determine materiality and decide what obligations follow — everything downstream depends on that call being made first
The regulator, because the 72-hour clock starts immediately regardless of internal process
The general public via a press release, to get ahead of leaks
items.explanation: Internal escalation comes first because legal/exec are the ones who assess materiality and trigger every subsequent obligation — regulatory notification and customer disclosure both depend on that internal determination happening first. Going to customers or the public before internal legal has assessed the situation risks disclosing something inaccurate or premature.
items.reference:
Internal
full detail, first call
Regulator
fixed legal deadline
Customers
without undue delay, once confirmed

Why: same facts, different audience, different timing and content.

items.prompt: Why does the customer notification generally go out after the regulatory one, rather than at the same time or before?
choices: Because customers legally have no right to know about a breach

Because customer-facing disclosure benefits from a more confirmed, unresolved-uncertainty-free scope than the earlier regulatory filing requires, and telling customers with unconfirmed or shifting facts can be as damaging as telling them late
Because regulators require companies to keep customers uninformed
There's no real reason, it's purely a historical convention
items.explanation: The regulatory filing can proceed on a preliminary but good-faith scope, since the process itself often expects updates as an investigation continues. Customer communication has less room for a walk-back — a wrong or incomplete early claim can damage trust more than a short additional delay to confirm the facts first.
items.reference:
Internal
full detail, first call
Regulator
fixed legal deadline
Customers
without undue delay, once confirmed

Why: same facts, different audience, different timing and content.

items.prompt: What does this unit mean by saying the three audiences need "different content," not just different timing?
choices: Nothing different — the exact same message should go to all three audiences for consistency

Internal needs full technical detail including open uncertainty; a regulator needs facts sufficient to meet a legal standard; customers need what happened to their own data and what to do next, without unresolved internal uncertainty cluttering the message
Only the regulator needs any real content; the others just need a generic notice
Content should be identical, only the delivery channel should differ
items.explanation: This is the same audience-awareness principle from `business-communication` applied under legal pressure: the same underlying facts get filtered differently for what each audience actually needs to act on. A customer doesn't need Northlake's internal debugging detail; legal needs exactly that detail plus the open questions still being resolved.
items.reference:
Internal
full detail, first call
Regulator
fixed legal deadline
Customers
without undue delay, once confirmed

Why: same facts, different audience, different timing and content.

items.prompt: Northlake's compromise began 11 days before detection, but the 72-hour disclosure clock only had a few hours elapsed by the time they filed on Day 13. Why doesn't the clock include those 11 undetected days?
choices: Because GDPR's 72-hour window starts at awareness of the breach, not at when the breach actually began
Because the clock only counts business days, excluding the 11 days entirely
Because the clock is measured from when the vulnerability was originally introduced
Because 72 hours is a rolling average across the whole incident
items.explanation: GDPR's window is explicitly anchored to awareness — the moment the organization becomes aware a breach has (likely) occurred — not the moment it started. This is exactly why fast, thorough detection matters so much: the clock effectively doesn't start ticking until someone notices, however long the attacker was actually inside beforehand.
items.reference:
Day 1: compromise begins. Day 11, 09:00: awareness confirmed, clock starts. Day 13, 06:40: regulator notified — inside 72 hours of awareness, not of Day 1

Why: the clock rewards fast detection, not fast attacks.

items.prompt: A team spends 5 extra days in ambiguous, inconclusive analysis before finally confirming a breach occurred. Does that delay count against their 72-hour window?
choices: Yes, every day of any investigation always counts against the 72 hours

Not directly against the 72-hour window itself, since that only starts at confirmed awareness — but the delay isn't free: it's still 5 more days the attacker may have had, and stalling analysis specifically to avoid triggering the clock would likely be viewed as bad faith
No, analysis time is always fully excluded no matter how long it takes or why
It depends only on how large the company is
items.explanation: Literally, the clock starts at confirmed awareness, so genuine investigation time before that point isn't counted against the 72 hours. But this isn't a loophole to game — dragging out analysis specifically to delay the clock's start, rather than because genuine uncertainty existed, undermines the entire point of the requirement and carries its own risk if that pattern becomes visible later.
items.reference:
Day 1: compromise begins. Day 11, 09:00: awareness confirmed, clock starts. Day 13, 06:40: regulator notified — inside 72 hours of awareness, not of Day 1

Why: the clock rewards fast detection, not fast attacks.

items.prompt: Why does this unit argue blameless post-mortems matter MORE for security incidents than for a typical engineering outage?
choices: They don't — the two are exactly the same in every respect

Because security incidents disproportionately involve a human decision made under real, adversarial pressure, and a blame culture specifically discourages the early, ambiguous reporting ("I think I clicked something") that catches things before they get much worse
Because security post-mortems are legally required to omit all human involvement
Because outages never involve human decisions, only security incidents do
items.explanation: Both kinds of post-mortems benefit from blamelessness, but security incidents raise the stakes: an attacker is actively exploiting the gap between policy and real human behavior under pressure. A culture that punishes admitting "I might have clicked something bad" doesn't close that gap — it just delays anyone finding out about it until the damage is much larger.
items.reference:
Blameless: "the pipeline allowed an unreviewed postinstall script to run" — fixable. Not blameless: "the engineer should have been more careful" — not fixable, and discourages the next report

Why: naming a person doesn't fix a system gap, and it discourages future reporting.

items.prompt: A post-mortem draft states the factual timeline precisely, including exactly which engineer approved a service account's broad scope months earlier, but frames it as a system gap rather than a personal failing. Is this consistent with a blameless approach?
choices: No — blameless means the person's involvement must be omitted from the record entirely

Yes — chain-of-custody-grade factual precision (who did what, when) can coexist with blamelessness; the distinction is whether the write-up frames it as a fixable system/process gap or as a personal character failing
No — blameless means every fact must be softened or made vague
Yes, but only if the engineer involved personally approves the wording first
items.explanation: Blameless doesn't mean vague or fact-free — a defensible record, sometimes for legal reasons, needs precise facts. What it means is separating "what happened, factually" from "whose fault this is, morally": the same precise fact (this account's scope was approved without a later review step) supports a fixable action item without needing to frame it as an individual's failing.
items.reference:
Blameless: "the pipeline allowed an unreviewed postinstall script to run" — fixable. Not blameless: "the engineer should have been more careful" — not fixable, and discourages the next report

Why: naming a person doesn't fix a system gap, and it discourages future reporting.

items.prompt: The `flagAnomalousSessions` function flags sessions using overnight timing AND an unrecognized source IP. What real attacker behavior would this rule structurally fail to catch?
choices: An attacker who exfiltrates during business hours from a known-good, trusted internal IP address
An attacker exfiltrating at 2am from a brand-new, never-seen IP — this is exactly what the rule is built to catch
Nothing — the rule catches every possible exfiltration pattern
An attacker who never logs in at all
items.explanation: This rule's two conditions (overnight timing, unrecognized IP) are exactly the pattern Northlake's real incident matched — but an attacker exfiltrating during business hours from a compromised machine that's already inside the trusted IP range would pass both checks and never be flagged. A detection rule only catches the specific signal it's built to look for; this is a real structural gap, not a bug to be quietly patched over without acknowledging the trade-off.
items.reference:
Rule catches: overnight + unrecognized IP. Rule misses: business-hours access from a trusted/already-compromised internal IP

Why: a detection rule only sees the signal it was built to look for.

items.prompt: What's a more robust improvement to `flagAnomalousSessions` that would catch a wider range of anomalies than the current overnight-plus-unfamiliar-IP rule?
choices: Removing the overnight check entirely, since it's the least useful condition
Adding a per-actor volume baseline (flag when an account's export volume is far above its own historical normal), independent of whether the source IP is already trusted
Only checking source IP and dropping every other signal
There's no possible improvement — this detection approach has a hard ceiling
items.explanation: A volume-baseline check (this account normally exports under 50 records, this session exported 410) catches the anomaly regardless of source IP or time of day — it's a genuinely independent signal from the current rule's two conditions, which is what makes it a real improvement rather than a tweak to the same blind spot.
items.reference:
Rule catches: overnight + unrecognized IP. Rule misses: business-hours access from a trusted/already-compromised internal IP

Why: a detection rule only sees the signal it was built to look for.

items.prompt: What does hashing the raw log file at collection time (`sealEvidence`) actually protect against?
choices: It protects against the log file being lost entirely
It lets anyone later prove whether the exact bytes used in the investigation match what was originally collected — any edit, even one byte, changes the hash completely
It automatically encrypts the log file so no one else can read it
It speeds up how fast the log can be parsed
items.explanation: A cryptographic hash is a fingerprint of the exact bytes at the moment it was taken. It doesn't prevent loss or unauthorized reading — it lets someone later verify integrity: re-hash the file and compare against the sealed value, and any change at all (even one character) produces a completely different hash, making tampering detectable rather than just theoretically possible.
items.reference:
sealEvidence(rawLog, 'dana@northlake', ts) → { sha256, collectedBy, collectedAt } — verifyEvidenceIntact() re-hashes and compares later

Why: a hash makes tampering detectable, not merely theoretically wrong.

items.prompt: Three weeks after collection, someone on the legal team asks Dana to prove the log used in the post-mortem is the same one collected at 02:19 on Day 11, unedited. What lets her answer that with evidence rather than just her word?
choices: Nothing — there's no way to prove a log file wasn't edited after the fact
Re-hashing the current file and comparing it against the sealed hash recorded at 02:19 — a match proves the bytes are identical to what was originally collected
Asking everyone on the team to vouch for her honesty
The file's last-modified timestamp alone, which can't be altered
items.explanation: `verifyEvidenceIntact` is exactly this check: re-hash the file as it exists now, compare to the hash sealed at collection time. A match is strong evidence the bytes are unchanged (file timestamps, by contrast, are trivially editable and prove nothing on their own).
items.reference:
sealEvidence(rawLog, 'dana@northlake', ts) → { sha256, collectedBy, collectedAt } — verifyEvidenceIntact() re-hashes and compares later

Why: a hash makes tampering detectable, not merely theoretically wrong.

items.prompt: A new incident: an attacker is actively dumping a full customer table right now, at high volume, with no durable request log capturing what's being taken. Per the runbook, what's the right call?
choices: Preserve the session to capture forensic detail, since nothing is logged yet
Isolate immediately — active, high-volume exfiltration routes straight to short-term containment regardless of logging gaps; the cost of more data leaving right now outweighs the forensic value here
Wait for legal approval before taking any action
Do nothing until the dump finishes on its own
items.explanation: The runbook's first branch is explicit: active, high-volume exfiltration in progress goes straight to immediate containment, full stop — the missing durable log actually strengthens (not weakens) the case for cutting it off fast, since there's nothing yet protecting against continued loss besides stopping the session itself.
items.reference:
Runbook step 2: active/high-volume → isolate now. Slow/durable-logged → isolate now. Unclear + real volatile-evidence value → brief capped preservation

Why: the runbook exists so this call doesn't have to be reasoned from scratch at 2am.

items.prompt: Per the runbook, at what point should evidence be sealed (hashed and timestamped)?
choices: Only after the post-mortem is fully written, weeks later
Before anyone starts drawing conclusions from the pulled logs — sealing happens right after containment, as its own explicit step, not as an afterthought once analysis is already underway
Sealing evidence is optional and can be skipped if the team trusts each other
Only if law enforcement specifically requests it
items.explanation: The runbook places sealing right after containment, deliberately before conclusions get drawn from the evidence — sealing late (e.g., after the team has already been analyzing an unsealed copy for hours) weakens the chain of custody, since there's no proof the analyzed copy matches whatever gets sealed afterward.
items.reference:
Runbook step 2: active/high-volume → isolate now. Slow/durable-logged → isolate now. Unclear + real volatile-evidence value → brief capped preservation

Why: the runbook exists so this call doesn't have to be reasoned from scratch at 2am.

items.prompt: Northlake's post-mortem's root cause is written as "the service account had standing read access broader than its job required" rather than "the attacker had a working password." Why is the former the better root cause?
choices: Because passwords being compromised is rare and unlikely to recur, so it's not worth analyzing

Because "the attacker had a working password" isn't something the team controls — credentials do get compromised sometimes — while the account's excess scope is a controllable factor that determined how much damage that compromise could do
Because naming the credential type is legally required in every post-mortem
There's no meaningful difference between the two framings
items.explanation: A good root cause points at something the team can actually change. Credential compromise is a risk every system has to assume will happen sometimes (people reuse passwords) — it's not a controllable root cause on its own. The account's excessive scope, on the other hand, is squarely something Northlake controlled and is exactly what turned one compromised password into 3,650 exposed records instead of a much smaller number.

choices: It's a gap — a proper post-mortem must always name who caused the problem
Intentional — accountability for a system gap is expressed as a fixable action item with a clear owner going forward, not as a name attached to how the gap originally came to exist

It's a gap, but only because the document should have included performance review consequences
items.explanation: This is the core mechanism of a blameless post-mortem: accountability doesn't disappear, it relocates — from "who is at fault for the past" to "who owns making sure this specific gap is closed going forward." That's a stronger, more actionable form of accountability than naming a person for something that, in Northlake's case, was a scope-approval process gap more than an individual failing.

items.prompt: Implement `groupByActorAndIp(entries)`: given an array of log entry objects `{ ts, actor, sourceIp }` (already sorted by `ts` ascending), group consecutive entries that share the same `actor` AND `sourceIp` into sessions. Return an array of `{ actor, sourceIp, count }` objects, one per contiguous run — a new group starts whenever `actor` or `sourceIp` changes from the previous entry, even if the same combination reappears later.

splits into two groups when sourceIp changes

items.explanation: This is the core of `groupIntoSessions` simplified: walk the sorted entries once, and only merge into the current group when both `actor` and `sourceIp` match the immediately preceding entry. Because the check is against the *last* group, not "has this combination ever appeared," the same actor+IP reappearing later (after an intervening different combination) correctly starts a brand-new group rather than merging back into the earlier one — which matters for telling apart two genuinely separate sessions from the same source.

items.prompt: Implement `isOvernight(isoTimestamp)`: return `true` if the UTC hour of the given ISO timestamp string is between 1 and 4 inclusive (the overnight window used by Northlake's anomaly rule), `false` otherwise. Use `Date` and `getUTCHours()`.

tests.description: boundary hour 5 does not count as overnight

items.explanation: A direct range check on `getUTCHours()`. The boundary conditions matter here specifically because anomaly rules like this one live or die on their exact thresholds — a session at 04:59 flags, one at 05:00 doesn't, and a real attacker who learns the threshold could deliberately time exports just outside it, which is itself a reason not to rely on a single, narrow rule like this one alone.

Why: exact thresholds are exactly what an attacker would probe for and try to slip under.

This is the volume-baseline check that catches anomalies `flagAnomalousSessions`'s IP-and-time-only rule misses (see the checkpoint in the deep dive).

exactly at the threshold does not count as exceeding it

items.explanation: Simple on its own, but this check is independent of source IP or time of day — which is exactly what makes it a genuine improvement rather than a variation on the same blind spot as the overnight-plus-IP rule: an attacker exfiltrating from a trusted IP during business hours still can't avoid a volume spike relative to that account's own history, unless they also throttle down to blend in, which caps how much damage they can do per unit time either way.

items.prompt: Implement `classifyContainment({ activeHighVolume, alreadyDurablyLogged })` following the runbook's decision tree: return `'isolate-now'` if `activeHighVolume` is `true`; otherwise return `'isolate-now'` if `alreadyDurablyLogged` is `true`; otherwise return `'preserve-briefly'`.

tests.description: active high-volume always isolates now, regardless of logging
slow trickle with durable logs isolates now (Northlake's real case)
not active/high-volume and not durably logged preserves briefly

items.explanation: This encodes the runbook's actual branching: active high-volume exfiltration always wins toward immediate isolation regardless of logging state, since ongoing loss outweighs forensic value. When it's not active/high-volume, durable logging removes the case for preservation (nothing left to gain by waiting) and also routes to isolation. Only when neither condition holds — genuinely unclear, and nothing already captured — does the narrow preserve-briefly branch apply.
items.reference:
Runbook: active/high-volume → isolate-now. Slow + already durably logged → isolate-now. Neither → preserve-briefly (capped)

Why: encoding the runbook as a function is what makes the 2am call fast and consistent, not reasoned from scratch each time.
